payload.sensitivity:
VERDICT: WEIGHT-SENSITIVE, and I am not going to call it robust when it is not. X3 leads X1 by 5 weighted points out of ~106. Three plausible perturbations flip it, and I hunted for them rather than for reassurance.

FLIP 1 - RAISE C4 (structured output) FROM 4 TO 5, OR SCORE X3's C4 AT 3 INSTEAD OF 4. Either flips the decision back to X1. CREDIBILITY: MODERATE-TO-HIGH, and this is the one that worries me. X3's C4 score of 4 rests on a probe I ran on ONE repository, ONE ref, and ASCII-ish content that my own probe then mangled by reading latin1. If NUL-separated parsing turns out fragile on real content - unusual encodings, very long lines, binary-ish files - the score is wrong and X1 wins. This is a live doubt, not a hypothetical, and it goes to M5 as a spike rather than being argued away here.

FLIP 2 - THE UNTRACKED-FILES DEFAULT PROVES UNFIXABLE OR AWKWARD. If including untracked files by default turns out to carry a real cost - performance, noise from build output, surprising interactions with ignore rules - then X3's C1 FRESHNESS becomes conditional, and C1 is a VETO. A veto failure does not cost points; it eliminates. CREDIBILITY: LOW-TO-MODERATE. git grep --untracked exists and is designed for exactly this, but I have not run it, and 'reading back what you just wrote' is the agent's single most common pattern, so a partial failure here is disproportionately damaging.

FLIP 3 - C5 (one implementation per job) DROPS FROM 5 TO 3. X3's biggest margin comes from C5, and C5's weight is my reading of an owner ruling about duplicate code. If the owner meant that ruling more narrowly - do not keep a dead fallback, rather than never use two tools for one job - then C5 deserves less weight and X1 wins on C4 and C6. CREDIBILITY: MODERATE. This is an interpretation of intent, and interpretations of intent are exactly what I got wrong three times yesterday. Named so the owner can correct it at gate_release rather than having it buried in a score.

WHAT DOES NOT FLIP IT, checked deliberately: no reweighting rescues X2 - its deficit is on C7 at weight 5 against a gain on C8 at weight 2, so C8 would have to outweigh C7 for X2 to win, which contradicts the register. And no reweighting rescues the DATUM: it fails a veto, and vetoes are not weights.

HONEST SUMMARY: the decision is CORRECT ON TODAY'S EVIDENCE and it is NOT SAFE FROM ITS OWN ASSUMPTIONS. Two of the three flips are settled by spikes I am about to run; the third is settled by the owner. That is the truthful position, and it is better than a robustness claim I would have to walk back.
payload.tripwires:
TWO MINTED as RAID watch-items with fallbacks, plus two flips routed to M5 spikes rather than to the register - because a question a spike will answer this milestone belongs in the spike, not in a watch list.

se.raid-git-grep-tracked-files-only (risk, agent) - FLIP 2 made concrete. git grep searches tracked files by default, so a file the agent just created and has not staged is INVISIBLE - aimed precisely at the agent's dominant pattern. RULED NOW rather than left as a flag to remember: untracked files are INCLUDED BY DEFAULT for working-tree searches and the caller opts OUT. A flag that must be remembered is a defect waiting for the one time it is not. Trigger: a search finding nothing while the caller can see the file. Test: create a file, leave it unstaged, search its content, expect a hit.

se.raid-a-requirement-may-yet-demand-ripgrep (assumption, agent) - FLIP 1's long tail, and the ceiling this decision accepted. git grep cannot match across lines, gives no submatch spans, and cannot search ignored files. The first requirement asking for any of those OVERTURNS the decision rather than bending around it - and the analysis is already recorded, so the revisit is a decision to re-run, not research to redo. Explicitly forbidden in the trigger: bending git grep around a multiline need with heuristics, which would recreate the hand-rolled searcher this iteration exists to delete.

ROUTED TO M5 INSTEAD OF THE REGISTER: (a) the NUL-parsing robustness that FLIP 1 turns on - one spike over real content, unusual encodings and long lines settles it, and if it fails the winner changes before any code is written; (b) whether semantic matching picks the rules that bind a state - X2's survival rests on it, and it must be measured before X2 is discarded.

ROUTED TO THE OWNER: FLIP 3, my reading of the no-duplicate-code ruling as 'never two tools for one job' rather than 'no dead fallback'. That interpretation carries the winner's largest margin, and misreading intent is the exact failure I made three times yesterday. It is surfaced at gate_release, not buried in a weight.
